intro: Lazur is a Google Docs voice typing alternative for Mac that works in any app, not only in Google Docs. Google's version types only inside Google Docs and Slides speaker notes, in Chrome, Edge or Safari. Lazur dictates at the cursor in Mail, Notes and other Mac apps, and it answers questions about your screen out loud. This page covers what each tool does, what it costs and where each one falls short.
tldr: Google Docs voice typing works inside Google Docs and Slides speaker notes only, in Chrome, Edge or Safari.
Lazur dictates in any Mac app when you hold fn, and it answers questions about your screen out loud.
Pick Google's tool if you write almost everything in Docs and want nothing else installed.
Pick Lazur if you move between Mac apps and want help with what is on screen. The trial is 3 days, then Pro is $18/month.

blocks.text: Google Docs voice typing or Lazur: the short answer

If you write almost everything in Google Docs, Google's built-in tool may be all you need. If you also write in Mail, Notes, Messages or a browser form, it stops at the edge of Docs. That is where Lazur comes in. It is built for the whole Mac, not one editor.
What Google Docs voice typing does

Google's help page treats voice typing as a feature of Docs. In Docs, choose Tools > Voice typing, then click the microphone. In Slides, the equivalent path is Tools > Dictate speaker notes. The page lists these pieces.

items: Spoken punctuation: period, comma, exclamation point, question mark, new line and new paragraph.
Commands for selecting words and paragraphs, formatting text and changing color.
Commands for editing, navigation, corrections and tables.
More than 100 languages and regional variants, such as English (US), English (UK), Spanish (Spain) and Japanese.
Voice commands work only in English. Your account language and your document language must both be English.

blocks.text: The language rule trips up many people. Dictation works in many languages, but the voice commands do not. If you dictate in Spanish, check whether you need the commands before you rely on them.
How to turn on Google Docs voice typing on a Mac

items: Open a document in Google Docs in Chrome, Edge or Safari. Google lists these three browsers for voice typing.
In Docs, choose Tools > Voice typing.
Click the microphone and allow the browser to use it when it asks.
Speak your sentence. Say “new paragraph” or “period” for punctuation.
If the microphone does nothing, open Settings > Privacy and security > Site settings > Microphone in Chrome and check that Google Docs is allowed.

blocks.text: Work accounts add one more check. Google's help page says an administrator can turn voice typing off. If the feature is missing, ask your IT team before you troubleshoot your own Mac.
How Lazur dictates in any Mac app

Lazur lives in the notch at the top of your screen. Hold fn and talk. Your words appear at the cursor in whichever app is active. Lazur dictates clean, formatted text, so you do not need to fix punctuation by hand every time.

Snippets, a personal dictionary and clipboard slots sit on top of dictation. Use the personal dictionary for names and terms that come out wrong. Use clipboard slots when you need to paste the same text again later.
How Lazur answers questions about your screen
Dictation is only half of Lazur. The other shortcut is ⌥ ⌘. Hold Option and Command together, then ask about anything on screen. Lazur answers out loud.

Ask where something is, and Lazur draws a circle and a label around it. Ask how to do something, and Lazur guides you one click at a time. It waits for each click. Lazur does not click buttons, edit files or operate other apps for you. You do the clicking. Lazur does the pointing and the explaining.
When Google Docs voice typing is the better pick

Google's version has real strengths. Docs is open to anyone with a Google Account, according to Google's product page. You install nothing beyond a supported browser. Its language list is long, with more than 100 languages and regional variants.

items: You write nearly everything in Google Docs or Slides speaker notes.
You want nothing installed beyond Chrome, Edge or Safari.
You dictate in one of the many languages on Google's list and do not need voice commands.
You already run Google Workspace, and your admin has turned voice typing on.

blocks.text: Slides is a good case. If you present from Google Slides, Tools > Dictate speaker notes is the direct route into your notes. Google built that option for the job, so start there.

A Pocket-lint reviewer tested the feature on a laptop in October 2025. They found setup straightforward. They liked the voice commands for selecting, copying and pasting. That is one reviewer on one laptop, so read it as a data point.
When Lazur is the better pick
Lazur fits the moment your hands leave Docs. That happens when you switch apps in the middle of a task.

items: You switch between Mail, Notes, a browser and a document during one task.
You get stuck in a Mac app and want something to point at the right button.
You want to ask what a message or a menu means and hear the answer out loud.
You want timers, Apple Reminders, Calendar events, notes and music by voice too.
You want research done in the background, in Lazur's own Chrome tabs, with a summary and a report.

blocks.text: Worked example: one afternoon across three apps

Say you are drafting a project update in Google Docs. You dictate the opening by voice, and that part works well in Docs. Then the review date sits in a calendar invite on your screen, and you need one fact from a web page.

With Docs voice typing alone, you stop dictating, switch to Calendar, read the date, switch back and type it. With Lazur, you hold ⌥ ⌘ while the invite is on screen and ask when the review is. Lazur answers out loud. Then you hold fn and dictate the sentence at your cursor.
There is one catch. Lazur looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. If the invite sits in a window you already closed, Lazur cannot see it. Open the window first, then hold the key.
Privacy: what happens to your voice and screen

Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. When it answers, audio and the screenshot go to AI providers. They are not stored, and content is never used to train AI models. Lazur keeps a memory of what you asked and did, on your Mac.

Google's pages are less specific. The Docs help page says the browser controls the speech-to-text service and sends recognized text to Docs or Slides. It does not say whether an internet connection is needed. It does not say whether recognition runs on your Mac.

Google's general privacy policy says the company uses service providers to analyze and listen to samples of saved user audio to improve audio recognition technologies. That policy is not written for voice typing alone, and it sets no audio-specific retention period. Chrome lets you change or block microphone access under Settings > Privacy and security > Site settings > Microphone. Chrome's help page does not say whether speech audio goes to Google.
If client, medical or legal details are involved, read both policies first. Then decide which tool your data can pass through.
How accurate is dictation, and what the research says

Speed is the main reason people dictate. In a lab study by Ruan and colleagues, English speech entry was 2.93 times faster than a QWERTY keyboard on an iPhone 6 Plus. That is 153 words per minute against 52.

Errors tell a second story. The corrected error rate was 5.30 percent for speech and 11.22 percent for the keyboard. But the uncorrected error rate in the final text was higher for speech, at 1.30 percent against 0.79 percent. Speech is faster, and you still need to read what it wrote.
That study tested phone keyboards in 2016 and 2017. It did not test Google Docs or Lazur. Treat it as evidence about speech input in general, not a score for either product.

Individual reviews show the rough edges. One Pocket-lint reviewer said Google's tool often misheard docs as dogs, and that the lag was irritating. The same reviewer said typing the old-fashioned way was still way faster and more accurate.

Test it on your own work before you choose. Dictate the same three paragraphs in each tool, then count how many words you had to fix. Try the [speaking vs typing test](/tools/speaking-vs-typing-test) and the [dictation accuracy checker](/tools/dictation-accuracy-checker) on your own sentences as well.
Mistakes people make when they switch

items: Expecting Google voice typing to work in Mail, Notes or Messages. It works in Docs and in Slides speaker notes.
Blocking the microphone in Chrome, then assuming the feature is broken.
Leaving the account or document language set to something other than English, then wondering why commands fail.
Running two dictation tools on the same key. Lazur dictates on fn, so change the other tool's shortcut first.
Expecting Lazur to do the clicking. It points and guides you one click at a time, and it waits for each click.
Asking about a window you already closed. Lazur sees the screen only while you hold the key.

blocks.text: Edge cases that change the answer

A few situations flip the choice. If your Mac is managed by work, an admin may have turned voice typing off. If you dictate in a language outside Google's list, Google will not help. If you need answers about what is on screen, Google's voice typing page lists nothing for that.
Words and names are another edge case. The help page does not list a personal dictionary for voice typing. Lazur has one. Add names and jargon once, then check the first few drafts.

If all you need is free built-in dictation outside Docs, read [Lazur vs Apple Dictation on Mac](/compare/lazur-vs-apple-dictation) before you decide. For more options, see [Google Docs voice typing alternatives for Mac](/alternatives/google-voice-typing).
Pricing: what each one costs

Google does not show a separate price for Docs voice typing on the pages we checked. Docs is open to anyone with a Google Account. Google's business pricing covers Workspace plans, priced per user. Check their pricing page before you decide, because the cost depends on whether you use a personal or work account.

Lazur has a 3-day Pro trial with no credit card. The trial starts when you first open the app. After that, Pro costs $18/month, or $15/month billed annually. Power costs $120/month, or $96/month billed annually.

Pro includes 250 AI actions, and Power includes 1,000. Dictation is unlimited on both plans. So the action count matters when you ask questions or ask for guided help. Check the [pricing page](/pricing) for the current terms.
How to choose and what to do next

Start with a week of your own work. Each time you leave Docs to type something else, write it down. If you almost never leave, Google's tool may be enough. If you leave often, the trial shows you whether Lazur earns its place.

items: Download Lazur from the [download page](/download), open it and start the trial.
In Mail or Notes, hold fn and dictate two sentences. Read the result.
With a web page open, hold ⌥ ⌘ and ask where the search box is.
In Google Docs, open Tools > Voice typing and dictate the same two sentences.
Compare the results and keep the tool you would reach for on your next task.

blocks.text: You can keep both. Lazur uses fn for dictation and ⌥ ⌘ for questions. Google's microphone sits inside Docs, so the two do not compete for a key.
What Lazur does not do

Lazur is not connected to Google Docs, and it is not a plugin or add-in for any app. It does not click buttons, edit files or operate other apps for you. Use it for the words and for the guidance, and keep the clicking in your own hands.

Lazur runs on macOS, on Apple silicon and Intel Macs. Windows is planned, not available. Google's help page lists the latest Chrome, Edge and Safari on desktop. One Pocket-lint test said voice typing did not work on Android.

faq.question: Is Lazur a good Google Docs voice typing alternative?
faq.answer: If you want more than dictation, yes. Lazur dictates in any Mac app when you hold fn, and it answers questions about your screen out loud when you hold ⌥ ⌘. If you only dictate inside Google Docs, Google's built-in tool is a fair choice.

faq.question: Does Google Docs voice typing work outside Google Docs?
faq.answer: No. Google's help page ties it to Google Docs and to Slides speaker notes. It works in the latest Chrome, Edge and Safari on desktop. For Mail, Notes or other Mac apps, you need a different tool.

faq.question: Can I use Lazur and Google Docs voice typing together?
faq.answer: Yes. Lazur dictates on hold fn and answers questions on hold ⌥ ⌘. Google's voice typing starts from Tools > Voice typing inside Docs, so the two do not share a shortcut.

faq.question: How long is the Lazur free trial?
faq.answer: The trial is 3 days, and it needs no credit card. It starts when you first open the app. After that, Pro costs $18/month, or $15/month billed annually.

faq.question: Does Google Docs voice typing work in languages other than English?
faq.answer: Yes, for dictation. Google's help page lists more than 100 languages and regional variants. Voice commands work only in English, and your account and document language must both be English.

faq.question: Does Lazur send my voice and screen to AI providers?
faq.answer: When you ask a question, audio and a screenshot go to AI providers so Lazur can answer. They are not stored, and content is never used to train AI models. Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut.

verdict: Pick Google Docs voice typing if almost all your dictation happens inside Google Docs, you want nothing installed, and you dictate in one of its supported languages. Pick Lazur if you move between Mac apps, want help with what is on screen, or want timers, reminders and research by voice too. If you are unsure, run the trial and compare both tools on your own work.
